## Frequently asked questions

**Is ElevenLabs free to use?**
Yes — the free plan includes 10,000 credits/month covering text-to-speech, speech-to-text, sound effects, and voice design across up to 3 projects. Fine for light use, but no commercial license or voice cloning.

**How much does ElevenLabs cost per month?**
Paid plans start at $5/month (Starter, 30,000 credits) and scale up to $990/month (Business, 6,000,000 credits), with custom Enterprise pricing above that. Annual billing discounts most tiers.

**What are ElevenLabs credits, and how fast do they run out?**
Credits are consumed based on the length and type of audio generated or transcribed, drawn from a shared monthly pool. How far they stretch depends on usage volume, so estimate your real output before picking a plan.

**Does ElevenLabs clone voices from a short audio sample?**
Instant voice cloning (Starter plan) works from a short sample in minutes, though quality varies. Professional voice cloning (Creator plan and up) needs more training audio but produces a closer, more stable match.

**Can I use ElevenLabs commercially?**
Commercial usage rights are included from the Starter plan upward; the Free plan does not include one.

**Is ElevenLabs good for developers?**
Yes — a REST API with official Python and TypeScript SDKs, plus a low-latency model (Eleven Flash v2.5) built for real-time use like voice agents, makes it a realistic option to build on rather than just a content tool.

**How does ElevenLabs handle data and voice privacy?**
Policies and compliance options (including HIPAA BAAs and custom SSO) vary by plan tier — check current terms and privacy documentation directly, especially before cloning real people's voices.

**What are the main alternatives to ElevenLabs?**
Other AI voice platforms include Murf AI, Play.ht, and WellSaid Labs, each with different strengths in narration style, pricing, or enterprise features. Compare actual per-minute costs at your expected usage volume, not just the advertised starting price.

Midjourney is one of the two or three AI image generators most creators default to, and for good reason: its outputs tend to have a distinct, painterly polish that other generators struggle to match straight out of the box. It's genuinely good, but it's also Discord/web-only, has no permanent free tier, and its command-based workflow has a real learning curve — so whether it's worth it depends heavily on how often you generate images and whether you need pixel-precise control.

| Best for | Concept art, illustration, mood boards, marketing visuals, stylized creative work |

## What Midjourney actually is

Midjourney is an independent research lab and AI image-generation service, self-funded and notably not backed by the usual big-tech investors that fund most other frontier AI labs. It generates images from text prompts (and now image inputs too) using its own proprietary diffusion models, iterated through several major versions — V4, V5.x, V6/V6.1, and the V7 and V8-series models that followed through 2025 and into 2026 — alongside specialized "Niji" versions tuned for anime and illustrated styles. Midjourney doesn't publish detailed architecture papers the way some competitors do, so specifics of the current model are known mainly through its own release notes rather than an academic paper.

Originally, the only way to use Midjourney was through Discord, typing `/imagine` commands into a bot and getting a 2x2 grid of images back. That's still supported, but since mid-2024 Midjourney has also offered its own web app with image editing, panning, zooming, region-based variation, and inpainting — now the more common way most subscribers actually work. There's still no official standalone desktop or mobile app; everything runs through a browser tab or Discord.

## Pricing

Midjourney sells access as a flat monthly or annual subscription rather than per-image credits, though heavier tiers effectively function as more generation time. As of Midjourney's own published plan structure, the tiers break down roughly like this:

| Plan | Monthly price | Annual price (per month, billed yearly) | Fast GPU time | Relax mode | Stealth mode |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Basic | $10 | ~$8 | ~3.3 hours/month | Not included | Not included |
| Standard | $30 | ~$24 | ~15 hours/month | Unlimited | Not included |
| Pro | $60 | ~$48 | ~30 hours/month | Unlimited | Included |
| Mega | $120 | ~$96 | ~60 hours/month | Unlimited | Included |

"Fast" hours are the GPU time used to generate images at normal speed; once you burn through your allotment, jobs either queue in slower "relax" mode (unlimited on Standard and above) or you buy extra fast-hours on top. Stealth mode, only on Pro and Mega, keeps your generations off the public community feed — useful for client work you don't want showing up in a public gallery search. All paid plans include commercial usage rights, though Midjourney's terms carve out extra requirements for companies above a certain revenue threshold, worth reading directly on its terms-of-service page if you're generating for a larger company.

Pricing, free-tier availability and feature allotments above were accurate as of this post's publish date but Midjourney has changed its plan structure before (it dropped free trials entirely in 2023, then briefly experimented with limited ones again) — always confirm current numbers on Midjourney's own account/billing page before subscribing.

There's no dedicated store entry for Midjourney on this site yet, so there's no coupon page to link to here.

## Features that actually differentiate it

**Default aesthetic quality.** This is the single biggest reason people pick Midjourney over free or cheaper alternatives. Even a short, unrefined prompt tends to produce something usable — good lighting, coherent composition, a level of "finish" that other generators often need heavier prompt engineering to match.

**Style Reference and Character Reference.** You can feed Midjourney a reference image and weight to pull its aesthetic (`--sref`) or a consistent character/subject (`--cref`) into new generations. This is genuinely useful for producing a series — book illustrations, a brand's visual identity, a recurring mascot — that need to look consistent across dozens of separate prompts.

**Vary (Region) and inpainting.** Rather than regenerating a whole image because one element is wrong, you can select just a region — a face, a background object — and regenerate only that part while the rest stays fixed, closing a gap that used to force people into Photoshop for small fixes.

**Niji models for anime/illustration.** A meaningfully different aesthetic target from the base model, tuned specifically for anime and stylized illustration rather than trying to be a generalist model that also does anime passably.

**Editable web app.** The panning/zooming/region-edit toolkit in the web interface, rather than juggling Discord slash commands, makes iterating on a specific image far less painful than the original Discord-only workflow — the biggest usability upgrade the product has had since launch.

## Who it's actually for

- **Solo creators and hobbyists** experimenting with AI art casually will likely find the $10 Basic plan tight — 3.3 fast hours a month disappears quickly once you start iterating, so budget for either relax-mode queue times or stepping up to Standard.
- **Freelancers and small studios** producing client-facing visuals (concept art, book covers, marketing assets) are the core audience for Standard or Pro — Pro's stealth mode matters if you're working on unreleased client projects you don't want appearing in Midjourney's public feed.
- **Agencies and teams generating at volume** across multiple campaigns or product lines are the target for Mega, where 60 fast-hours and stealth mode justify $120/month against running several separate lower-tier accounts.
- **Anyone needing precise, deterministic output** (exact text rendering, exact logo placement, pixel-level control) should treat Midjourney as a starting point, not a finishing tool — it's a probabilistic generator, not a design program, and will need touch-up work in an actual editor.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Strong default image quality with minimal prompt effort | No permanent free tier — every account needs a paid plan to generate |
| Style/character reference tools genuinely help visual consistency across a series | Discord-based origin still shows; the web app is better but community-feed culture bleeds through |
| Web app removes most of the old Discord-only friction | Fast-hour allotments run out quickly once you're iterating heavily |
| Niji models give a real second aesthetic lane for anime/illustration work | Text rendering inside images, while improved, is still not fully reliable |
| Commercial usage rights included on all paid plans | Lower tiers publish your generations to a public feed unless you're on Pro/Mega |

## Integrations and ecosystem

Midjourney doesn't offer a first-party public API for developers to build on top of — access is through the Discord bot or the official web app only, a real limitation if you wanted to wire image generation into your own app or automation pipeline (Zapier-style integrations exist only informally, via third parties automating the Discord interface, which are unsupported and can violate the terms of service). There's no native Slack, Notion or design-tool plugin either. If you specifically need programmatic, API-first image generation for a product you're building, look at API-first competitors instead. What Midjourney does integrate well with is Discord itself, and, informally, any workflow where you're happy to download finished PNGs into whatever design tool you already use.

## Where it's a strong fit

Midjourney earns its subscription price for anyone doing repeated concept art, mood-boarding, stylized marketing visuals, or illustration work where "looks great by default" matters more than exact control. Teams producing a steady stream of visual content — blog headers, ad creative, character concepts — get real value out of the reference tools once they've learned the prompt syntax, and the web app's editing tools have closed most of the gap that used to send people to a separate editor for small fixes.

## Where to think twice

Skip Midjourney, or at least don't lead with it, if you need a genuinely free tool with no ongoing cost — there isn't one, and free trials are inconsistent and often unavailable. Skip it too if you need API access to build image generation into your own product, since Midjourney has no supported developer API. Teams with strict compliance or enterprise data-handling requirements should check Midjourney's terms directly rather than assume formal enterprise contracts exist, since its support structure is still built primarily around individual and small-team subscriptions. And if exact, literal output — precise text, exact brand colors, pixel-perfect layout — matters more than aesthetic quality, a probabilistic generator like this will frustrate you; budget time for manual touch-ups regardless of which plan you pick.

## Bottom line

Midjourney remains one of the strongest choices for AI image generation if what you're after is polished, aesthetically strong output without needing to fight the tool for it. It's not the cheapest option and has no meaningful free tier, but the combination of default output quality, the reference tools for consistency across a series, and a genuinely improved web editing interface make the Standard or Pro plan a reasonable recurring cost for anyone who generates images regularly. If your use case is occasional or you need API access, look elsewhere first.

[Try Midjourney](/go/offer/midjourney)

## Frequently asked questions

**Does Midjourney have a free plan?**
No ongoing free tier exists as of this writing — every account needs an active paid subscription (Basic and up) to generate images. Midjourney has occasionally offered limited free trials in the past and pulled them due to abuse, so don't assume one will be available when you sign up.

**What's the cheapest way to try Midjourney?**
The $10/month Basic plan (or its discounted annual equivalent) is the lowest-cost entry point. Given the limited fast-hours on Basic, expect to spend most of your time in the slower relax-mode queue unless you upgrade.

**Can I use Midjourney images commercially?**
Yes, all paid plans include commercial usage rights for images you generate, though Midjourney's terms of service have extra requirements for larger companies above a specific revenue threshold — read the current terms directly before using output for a larger commercial venture.

**Does Midjourney keep my generations private?**
Only Pro and Mega plans include stealth mode, which keeps your generations off Midjourney's public community feed. On Basic and Standard, your prompts and images are visible in the public feed by default.

**Is Midjourney better than other AI image generators?**
"Better" depends on the use case — Midjourney generally has an edge on default aesthetic polish, but other generators may edge it out on exact prompt adherence, price, or having a genuinely free tier. If you need programmatic API access, competitors that offer a developer API are the better fit regardless of image quality.

**Do I need to use Discord to use Midjourney?**
No — since mid-2024 Midjourney has offered its own web app with image generation and editing built in, now the more common way most subscribers work. Discord access is still available if you prefer the original workflow.

**Is Midjourney beginner-friendly?**
It's approachable to start (type a prompt, get an image) but has a real learning curve to get consistently strong results — style weight, aspect ratio flags and reference-image syntax take some practice. Budget an hour or two of experimentation before judging fit.

**How often does Midjourney release new models?**
Midjourney has released major version updates roughly every several months to a year historically (V4 through the V7/V8-series), each generally improving prompt adherence, coherence and text rendering — check Midjourney's own changelog for the exact current model version.

body:
## A2 Hosting Review 2026: What Happened to the Brand, and Is It Worth It?

A2 Hosting no longer exists as an independent brand — it was acquired by World Host Group in January 2025 and rebranded as hosting.com in April 2025. The infrastructure, cPanel-based shared hosting, and account systems carried over; the old Startup/Drive/Turbo Boost/Turbo Max plans were simply renamed Starter/Plus/Pro/Max, with NVMe storage now standard on every tier instead of just the premium ones.

### At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $3.99/month (Starter, 1-year term) |
| Renewal price | Not published; independent reviews report a steep increase, commonly cited around $11-$28/month depending on tier |
| Uptime guarantee | 99.9% with service credits |
| Money-back guarantee | 30 days |
| Control panel | cPanel |
| Best for | Sites that want NVMe/LiteSpeed performance on an entry-level plan |

### What A2 Hosting actually is now

If you searched for "A2 Hosting" expecting to land on a2hosting.com, you'd have been redirected — the domain now forwards to hosting.com. World Host Group, which already owns several hosting brands, bought A2 Hosting in January 2025 and folded it into hosting.com a few months later as part of a broader consolidation. This isn't a shutdown: the shared hosting product, cPanel setup, and NVMe-backed infrastructure A2 was known for are still being sold, just under a new name and with a simplified four-tier lineup. Long-time A2 customers have reported a rockier transition period with support response times, though multiple 2026 reviews note that response times have recovered since.

For anyone comparing hosts today, this matters because pricing pages, coupon codes, and reviews still referencing "A2 Hosting Turbo" or "A2 Hosting Startup" are describing a product that has since been renamed and repriced — treat older A2-branded pricing screenshots as outdated.

### Pricing table

Pricing accurate as of September 2026 and subject to change — verify current rates at checkout.

| Plan (formerly) | Price | Storage | Websites |
|---|---|---|---|
| Starter (Startup) | $3.99/mo | 15GB NVMe | 1 |
| Plus (Drive) | $3.99/mo | 30GB NVMe | 2 |
| Pro (Turbo Boost) | $6.99/mo | 50GB NVMe | 10 |
| Max (Turbo Max) | $8.99/mo | 100GB NVMe | 100 |

All four tiers now include NVMe storage, LiteSpeed caching, unlimited bandwidth, unlimited databases, free SSL, and a free domain for the first year on annual terms — features that used to be split between A2's standard and Turbo lineups are now bundled into every plan.

### The real cost breakdown

The prices above are the introductory rate on a 1-year term, not what you'll pay indefinitely. hosting.com doesn't publish an exact renewal figure on its pricing page — a departure from A2's old habit of showing renewal pricing up front — but multiple independent reviews of the post-rebrand pricing report renewal invoices landing well above the intro rate, with figures cited in roughly the $11-$28/month range depending on the tier and term length chosen. Because the exact number isn't disclosed publicly, add the plan to your cart and check the renewal price hosting.com shows at checkout before you commit, rather than assuming the first-year price is permanent. The free first-year domain also reverts to a standard renewal price at the registrar rate once that year is up.

### Which plan should you choose

- **Choose Starter** if you're launching a single small site — a portfolio, a local business page, or a blog — and don't need room to grow beyond one domain.
- **Choose Plus** if you're running two small sites, or want a little more storage headroom than Starter without paying Pro pricing.
- **Choose Pro** if you're managing up to 10 sites, such as a freelancer or small agency hosting a handful of client sites on one account.
- **Choose Max** if you need capacity for many sites (up to 100) on a single plan — useful for a larger portfolio of low-traffic sites, though a single high-traffic site would outgrow shared hosting regardless of tier.

### Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| NVMe storage and LiteSpeed caching now included on every tier, not just premium ones | Exact renewal pricing isn't published — you have to check at checkout |
| cPanel, a control panel most site owners already know | Brand transition has caused confusion about which product you're actually buying |
| 30-day money-back guarantee | Some long-time A2 customers reported a dip in support quality right after the acquisition |
| Free domain and SSL on annual plans | Shared hosting still means shared server resources regardless of the rebrand |

### Support

hosting.com offers the support channels A2 customers were used to — live chat and a ticketing system are the primary channels for shared hosting customers. Reviews from 2026 indicate response times dipped during the immediate post-acquisition transition in 2025 but have since recovered; it's still worth checking current chat wait times before you buy if fast support response is a priority for you.

### Migration

Free website migration is included, continuing a feature A2 was known for. If you're moving from another cPanel-based host, migration tends to be the most straightforward, since hosting.com's shared plans run on the same control panel most budget hosts use — expect more manual work if you're migrating off a host with a custom, non-cPanel dashboard.

### Where it's a strong fit

- You want NVMe/LiteSpeed-class performance without paying for a premium "Turbo" tier — that's now the default across the board.
- You're comfortable with cPanel and want a familiar admin experience rather than a proprietary dashboard.
- You're consolidating several low-traffic sites onto one account and want the higher website-count ceiling the Pro or Max tiers offer.

### Where to think twice

- You want full pricing transparency before you commit — the lack of a published renewal rate means you have to dig for it at checkout.
- You specifically wanted to buy from "A2 Hosting" as a brand — that name no longer represents an independently operated company.
- You're deciding based on A2's older reputation for turbo-tier performance without checking that the product you'd actually be buying today is the renamed, restructured hosting.com lineup.

### Bottom line

The hosting product formerly sold as A2 Hosting is still a reasonable shared hosting option — NVMe storage and LiteSpeed caching across every tier is a genuine improvement over A2's old premium-only Turbo model, and the cPanel setup and 30-day guarantee carried over intact. The catch is the same one that dogs most budget hosts: the eye-catching intro price isn't the real long-term cost, and here it's compounded by hosting.com not publishing the renewal rate outright. If you go in expecting to check the renewal figure at checkout and budget for a multi-year cost rather than the first invoice, it's a solid pick for small-to-mid site counts on a familiar control panel.

### FAQs

**Is A2 Hosting still around?**
Not as an independent company. A2 Hosting was acquired by World Host Group in January 2025 and rebranded as hosting.com in April 2025. The a2hosting.com domain now redirects to hosting.com.

**What are A2's old plans called now?**
Startup became Starter, Drive became Plus, Turbo Boost became Pro, and Turbo Max became Max.

**What does hosting.com's shared hosting cost?**
Starter and Plus both start at $3.99/month, Pro at $6.99/month, and Max at $8.99/month, on a 1-year introductory term. Renewal pricing is higher but isn't published on the pricing page — confirm it at checkout.

**Does hosting.com use cPanel?**
Yes, shared hosting runs on the standard cPanel control panel, the same as it did under A2.

**Is there a free domain and SSL?**
A free domain is included for the first year on annual plans, and SSL certificates are free on all shared hosting plans.

**What's the money-back guarantee?**
30 days on new shared hosting purchases. It doesn't cover domain registrations/renewals or certain add-on services.

**Is migration free?**
Yes, free website migration is included, a feature that carried over from A2.

**Did support get worse after the A2-to-hosting.com transition?**
Some long-time A2 customers reported slower support response right after the January 2025 acquisition, but multiple 2026 reviews note response times have recovered since.

Bluehost is one of the longest-running mainstream web hosts, owned by Newfold Digital, and has been an officially recommended host on WordPress.org for years. It runs shared, WordPress-specific, VPS, dedicated and a newer cloud hosting line. The shared and WordPress plans use cPanel, the industry-standard control panel most hosting guides and tutorials are written for — a practical advantage if you'll ever need help from a non-Bluehost-specific source or want to move providers later, since cPanel accounts are broadly portable.

The advertised $3.99/month Starter price only applies if you prepay the full 36-month term up front — that's roughly $144 charged at checkout, not $3.99. Pay monthly or choose a shorter term instead, and the rate is meaningfully higher from day one.

**Choose Starter** if you're launching one small site — a blog, portfolio, or single-business page — and don't need more than 10GB of storage or multiple domains.

**Choose Business** if you're running several sites under one account, want a CDN included, or expect enough traffic that 50GB of storage and higher resource limits matter.

**Choose eCommerce Essentials** if you're building a store — it adds ecommerce-specific tooling on top of the Business plan's resources, though for a serious storefront it's worth comparing against dedicated ecommerce hosting or platforms before committing.

## Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Uses standard cPanel, not a proprietary dashboard | Lowest price requires a 36-month prepay |
| Free domain and SSL included in year one | Renewal prices are 1.5-2.5x the intro rate |
| Official WordPress.org recommended host | Free domain reverts to standard pricing after year one |
| 99.99% uptime SLA and 24/7 chat support | Cloud hosting tier drops cPanel entirely |

## Support

Trustpilot feedback is mixed on support wait times and consistency between agents, though most recent reviews describe support as responsive and able to resolve issues in one interaction.

Bluehost provides a website migration process for moving an existing site onto its hosting, including WordPress-specific migration tools. As with most hosts, free migrations are typically limited in scope (e.g. a single site) — check current terms before assuming a complex multi-site migration is included at no cost, and back up your existing site independently before starting any transfer.

## Where it's a strong fit

- First website or blog where cPanel familiarity and WordPress-specific guidance matter more than rock-bottom long-term pricing.
- Sites likely to need standard hosting features (email, staging, SSH) without paying for a higher-tier plan.
- Buyers comfortable prepaying multiple years to lock in the lowest rate and who won't be caught off guard by the renewal jump.

## Where to think twice

- If you want a flat, predictable monthly cost from month one, since Bluehost's advertised price is explicitly a limited-time new-customer rate.
- If you specifically want to avoid a long upfront commitment — the cheapest per-month rate is tied to the 36-month term, not to monthly billing.
- If you're set on Bluehost Cloud hosting and want cPanel — that product line doesn't include it.

## Bottom line

Bluehost remains a reasonable, well-established choice for a first website, mainly on the strength of cPanel, WordPress's own recommendation, and broad support coverage. The catch isn't hidden, but it is easy to skim past: the headline price is a 36-month-prepay, new-customer rate that renews at up to 2.5x higher. Go in planning around the renewal price, not the banner price, and Bluehost is a solid, unremarkable-in-a-good-way host. Go in expecting the intro price to hold, and renewal will feel like a bait-and-switch.

Check current deals on the [Bluehost coupon page](/coupons/bluehost), or compare it against other providers on our [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) page.

Yes — cPanel, one-click WordPress installs, and 24/7 chat support make it approachable for a first website, though the plan and pricing structure still rewards reading the fine print before buying.

**Does Bluehost use cPanel?**
Yes, on its shared, WordPress and VPS plans. Bluehost Cloud hosting is the exception and doesn't include cPanel.

Shared hosting renews at $9.99/month (Starter), $13.99/month (Business) or $21.99/month (eCommerce Essentials) — noticeably more than the introductory rate, which only applies to the first term.

**Does Bluehost offer a free domain?**
Yes, a free domain registration for the first year on new hosting plans. It renews at Bluehost's standard domain pricing afterward.

A 30-day money-back guarantee on hosting plans, letting you cancel within that window for a refund if it's not a fit.

**How does Bluehost handle site migrations?**
Bluehost offers migration support and WordPress-specific migration tools for moving an existing site over; free migrations are typically limited in scope, so confirm what's covered before a complex multi-site move.

**Is Bluehost better than Hostinger or Namecheap?**
It depends on priorities: Bluehost offers standard cPanel and WordPress.org's official recommendation, Hostinger uses its own simplified hPanel at a lower entry price, and Namecheap also runs cPanel with a longer-standing 30-day guarantee. Compare the specific renewal prices and storage limits for your use case rather than picking on brand alone.

**Can I pay monthly instead of prepaying years upfront?**
Bluehost's lowest advertised rate is tied to its longest (36-month) term. Monthly or shorter-term billing is typically available but at a higher effective rate — check the live pricing page for current monthly options.

## What DreamHost actually is

DreamHost is a web hosting company that's been operating since 1996, offering shared hosting, WordPress-optimized hosting (DreamPress), VPS, and dedicated servers. Unlike most budget hosts that license cPanel, DreamHost built its own control panel from scratch. It handles domains, email, databases, one-click installs and SSL from a single dashboard, but the interface and terminology differ from cPanel, so anyone migrating from a cPanel host will need a short adjustment period rather than a drop-in replacement.

DreamHost also positions itself around data privacy commitments (it publicly opposed government data requests in the past) and offers a free tier of WordPress hosting for qualifying nonprofits — a niche but genuine differentiator most budget hosts don't offer.

The advertised price is what you pay for the first year only, generally requiring at least an annual commitment upfront. Domain registration fees themselves are not covered by the money-back guarantee even if you cancel hosting.

- **Choose Launch** if you're running one to a handful of small sites (blogs, portfolios, local business sites) and don't need more than 25GB of storage — it's the cheapest entry point and covers most first-website use cases.
- **Choose Growth** if you're managing several sites (an agency with a handful of client sites, or a personal site plus a couple of side projects) and want double the storage and website allowance without jumping to VPS.
- **Choose Scale** if you're running many sites off one account, need the largest inode allowance DreamHost offers on shared hosting, or expect meaningfully more disk usage than the lower tiers allow — but at this price point it's worth comparing against a small VPS plan for the same money.

## Pros and cons

|---|---|

There's no inbound phone support line for general technical issues — DreamHost instead offers scheduled callbacks, which are prioritized in the support queue but not a substitute for calling in directly. If phone access matters to you, weigh that against hosts that do offer it.

DreamHost provides a free WordPress Automated Migration plugin, built with BlogVault, that moves site content, themes, plugins and configuration to DreamHost — DreamHost's own documentation says most migrations finish in under an hour, though larger or more complex sites can take longer. For a first site or a small handful of low-traffic sites, it's a reasonable choice as long as you plan for the renewal cost rather than being surprised by it.

30 days on shared hosting plans paid by credit card, per DreamHost's current pricing page; domain registration fees are excluded from any refund.

Yes, via its free Automated Migration plugin, which DreamHost says typically completes in under an hour for most WordPress sites. It doesn't support site builders like Wix or Squarespace.

Live chat is available 24/7 in English and Spanish. There is no general inbound phone support line; DreamHost offers scheduled callbacks instead.

body:
## SiteGround Review: Is It Worth the Price in 2026?

SiteGround is a solid pick if you value performance and support over the lowest possible price. It runs on Google Cloud, includes free daily backups on every plan, and holds a 4.9/5 rating from over 30,000 Trustpilot reviews. The catch: renewal prices jump 3-4x after your first term, so it suits buyers who plan to stay long-term and don't mind paying more than budget hosts once the intro period ends.

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting price | $3.99/mo (StartUp, first term) |
| Renewal price | $17.99/mo (StartUp) |
| Control panel | Site Tools (proprietary) |
| Uptime | Not independently guaranteed with SLA credits published on the plans page |
| Money-back guarantee | 30 days |
| Free domain | Yes, first year |
| Best for | WordPress sites, buyers prioritizing support and speed over lowest price |

Pricing above reflects rates as of this post's publish date (September 2026) and can change — check SiteGround's own pricing page for the current live rate before buying.

### What SiteGround actually is

SiteGround is a web hosting company founded in Bulgaria in 2004, now operating out of Sofia with additional offices in the US, UK and Spain. It hosts several million domains and is one of a small number of providers officially recommended by WordPress.org. In 2020 SiteGround moved its entire hosting infrastructure onto Google Cloud, running all sites on Google's SSD persistent storage — a detail the company leans on heavily in its marketing, since it's a genuine differentiator from hosts still running older bare-metal or generic cloud stacks.

Instead of cPanel, SiteGround built its own dashboard called Site Tools. It handles domains, email, SSL, backups, staging and site management in one place. It's a cleaner, more modern interface than cPanel for most tasks, but it means some tutorials and third-party guides written for cPanel won't map directly onto SiteGround's layout.

Beyond shared hosting, SiteGround also sells managed WordPress and WooCommerce hosting, and cloud hosting for larger, resource-intensive sites — all built on the same Site Tools panel and Google Cloud backend.

### Pricing table

| Plan | Websites | Storage | Intro price | Renewal price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| StartUp | 1 | 10 GB | $3.99/mo | $17.99/mo |
| GrowBig | Unlimited | 50 GB | $6.69/mo | $29.99/mo |
| GoGeek | Unlimited | 100 GB | $10.69/mo | $44.99/mo |

All three tiers include free SSL, a free domain for the first year, free daily backups with a 30-day history, a free CDN spanning 170+ locations, and 24/7 support. GrowBig adds on-demand backup copies and staging; GoGeek adds priority support, private DNS and Git-integrated staging — features aimed at developers and agencies managing client sites.

### The real cost breakdown

This is where SiteGround needs a clear-eyed look. The advertised $3.99/$6.69/$10.69 prices only apply to your first billing term (commonly 12 months). After that, plans renew at $17.99, $29.99 and $44.99 per month — a jump of roughly 3.5x to 4.5x over the intro rate. That's a steeper renewal increase than budget-tier hosts like Hostinger or Namecheap, where the multiplier is usually closer to 2-3x.

Practically, that means a StartUp plan costs about $48 for the first year but roughly $216/year every year after, if billed monthly at the renewal rate (annual prepay at renewal typically works out somewhat cheaper per month, but still well above the intro rate). If you're comparing hosts purely on sticker price, run the math on year two and year three, not just the signup screen — SiteGround's actual long-term cost is closer to a mid-tier managed host than a rock-bottom budget provider.

### Which plan should you choose

**Choose StartUp** if you're launching a single small site — a portfolio, a local business page, or a simple blog — and don't expect to add more sites soon. The 1-website cap is the main limitation; if you outgrow it, upgrading later is straightforward but resets your promotional pricing clock.

**Choose GrowBig** if you're running more than one site, want on-demand backup copies you can trigger manually before a risky update, or want staging environments to test changes before pushing live. This is SiteGround's most popular tier for a reason — it removes the single-site ceiling without jumping to GoGeek's developer-focused extras.

**Choose GoGeek** if you're an agency or developer managing multiple client sites, need Git-integrated staging, want priority ticket queues, or require the highest resource allocation SiteGround offers on shared hosting. It's overkill for a single personal site.

### Pros and cons

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Runs on Google Cloud infrastructure | Renewal prices are steep relative to budget hosts |
| Free daily backups included on every plan | StartUp plan caps you at 1 website |
| 4.9/5 rating across 30,000+ Trustpilot reviews | Custom Site Tools panel differs from cPanel-based tutorials |
| Officially recommended by WordPress.org | 30-day guarantee is shorter than some competitors' 45-90 day windows |
| Staging and Git integration on GrowBig/GoGeek | No published uptime SLA credits on the plans page |

### Support

SiteGround offers 24/7 support via live chat and ticket, plus phone support during business hours in several regions. GoGeek customers get access to a priority support queue, which is meant to reduce wait times for agencies managing time-sensitive client work. The high Trustpilot volume and score suggest support quality is a genuine strength rather than just marketing copy — it's one of the more consistently praised aspects across independent reviews.

### Migration

SiteGround provides a free WordPress site migration on GrowBig and GoGeek plans via its Migrator plugin, which handles most standard WordPress transfers automatically. StartUp customers and non-WordPress sites typically need to migrate manually or pay for assisted migration. If you're moving an existing WordPress site and want a hands-off transfer, GrowBig or above is the more practical entry point.

### Where it's a strong fit

SiteGround makes sense if you're hosting a WordPress site and want a provider WordPress.org itself vouches for, if you value daily backups and staging environments without paying extra for them, or if you're willing to pay renewal-tier pricing in exchange for consistently strong support and infrastructure. It's also a reasonable pick for small agencies on GoGeek, given the Git staging and priority support.

### Where to think twice

If your budget is fixed and you're price-sensitive past year one, the renewal jump makes SiteGround one of the more expensive shared-hosting options once the intro term ends — budget hosts with smaller renewal multipliers will cost meaningfully less over a 3-year horizon. The StartUp plan's single-website limit is also worth noting if you might add a second site later, since upgrading forfeits your existing promotional rate.

### Bottom line

SiteGround earns its reputation on infrastructure and support quality, backed by an unusually large and consistently positive review base. But it's not the cheapest option once you look past the first billing cycle — the renewal pricing is a real cost, not a footnote, and it should factor into your decision as much as the storage limits or feature list. If long-term reliability and support matter more to you than shaving a few dollars off monthly hosting, SiteGround is a reasonable choice. If you're optimizing purely for lowest total cost over several years, compare its renewal rates directly against competitors before committing.

See the [SiteGround coupon page](/coupons/siteground) for current offers, or browse [Web hosting deals](/category/hosting) to compare more providers.

Yes — Site Tools is a clean, guided dashboard, and SiteGround's WordPress installer and staging tools are straightforward even without prior hosting experience.

**Does SiteGround offer a free domain?**

Your plan renews at the standard rate — $17.99/mo (StartUp), $29.99/mo (GrowBig) or $44.99/mo (GoGeek) — rather than the introductory price, regardless of how long your initial prepay term was.

**Does SiteGround use cPanel?**
No. SiteGround built its own control panel, Site Tools, which replaces cPanel across all its hosting plans.

**How does SiteGround's migration process work?**
GrowBig and GoGeek customers get a free automated WordPress migration via SiteGround's Migrator plugin; other migrations are typically manual or require a paid migration service.

**What's SiteGround's money-back guarantee?**
30 days from signup, full refund, no long-term contract risk if it isn't a fit.

SiteGround runs on Google Cloud's infrastructure, which is generally associated with strong reliability, though the company doesn't publish a specific uptime SLA with credits on its plans page the way some hosts do.

Yes, you can upgrade from StartUp to GrowBig or GoGeek at any time, though doing so typically means paying the new plan's current rate rather than keeping your original promotional price.
